--- title: "" format: html: css: styles.css --- ::: {#inject-state .cell execution_count=2} ::: ::: {.hero} ::: {.kicker} A working paper on AI and monetary policy ::: # If you can fool the Fed's nowcast, you can move tens of billions of dollars. ::: {.subhead} Every major central bank now reads the economy in real time through machine-learning models that ingest scraped public-web data. We modeled what happens when an adversary contaminates the inputs. ::: ::: {.byline} By **John Blakeslee** · Updated April 2026 ::: ::: ::: {.lede} The Federal Reserve has a measurement problem, and it has had one for fifty years. In the late 1960s and through the 1970s, the period economists now call the Great Inflation, real-time output gaps were grossly understated. Policymakers saw slack where there was none. Between 1973 and 1975, as Athanasios Orphanides has shown, the federal funds rate sat roughly 300 basis points below what a Taylor rule run on accurate data would have prescribed. The misreading was not the only cause of runaway inflation. It was jet fuel. Three decades later, in 2008, the Fed misread the data the other way. Initial GDP figures missed the collapse by about five percentage points. The aggressive easing came late. ::: ::: {.timeline} ::: {.timeline-track} ::: {.timeline-events} ::: {.timeline-event} ::: {.dot} ::: ::: {.year} 1973 ::: ::: {.label} The Great Inflation ::: ::: {.stat} −300 bp below Taylor ::: ::: {.desc} Output gap mismeasured. Fed sat 300 bp too low for two years. ::: ::: ::: {.timeline-event} ::: {.dot} ::: ::: {.year} 2008 ::: ::: {.label} The Financial Crisis ::: ::: {.stat} −5.0 pp on initial GDP ::: ::: {.desc} Initial GDP missed the collapse by five percentage points. Easing came late. ::: ::: ::: {.timeline-event} ::: {.dot} ::: ::: {.year} 2024 ::: ::: {.label} The Pravda operation ::: ::: {.stat} 3.6 M articles ::: ::: {.desc} Russia poisons LLM-readable web at scale. Same attack surface as central-bank nowcasts. ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.lede .no-dropcap} Roberto Billi of the Riksbank put it plainly: "In practice, however, the output gap is a noisy signal of economic activity. Estimates of the output gap are often subject to large revisions, even long after the time policy is actually made." A study he co-authored found that between 1991 and 2010 the difference between the CBO's real-time estimates of the output gap and its eventual revisions ran from negative 3.3 percentage points to positive 3.0 percentage points. Orphanides put a number on the typical magnitude: 58 basis points of standard deviation on the first revision alone, with the maximum approaching 200. This is the inheritance modern central banking still carries. Now imagine the same problem, deliberately weaponized. ::: ::: {.pullquote} "A recurrent source of errors has been misperceptions of the state of the economy, the result of incorrect assessments of the economy's productive potential." ::: {.pullquote-attrib} Athanasios Orphanides ::: :::
::: {.lede} ## A new kind of attack surface Through the 2010s and 2020s, central banks pushed past the slow drip of official statistics. The Bank for International Settlements has tracked the shift in its annual reports for years. Every major central bank now runs some version of a real-time nowcast pipeline. The pipelines synthesize scraped price data, credit-card transaction aggregates, job-posting feeds, satellite imagery of major ports, and social-media sentiment. They produce daily-frequency estimates of output and inflation, well before the Bureau of Labor Statistics or the Bureau of Economic Analysis publish anything official. These pipelines have a property that traditional government statistics do not. ::: ::: {.pipeline} ### Two ways to measure the economy ::: {.pipeline-grid} ::: {.pipeline-col .bls} #### Traditional · BLS / BEA ##### Air-gapped, validated, slow - Mandatory establishment surveys - Encrypted transmission - Multi-stage internal validation - Blackout windows around release - Decades of audit infrastructure ::: {.verdict} Hard to tamper with. Lags by weeks or months. ::: ::: ::: {.pipeline-col .now} #### Real-time · Nowcast ##### Open-web ingestion, weak validation - Web-scraped price quotes - Card-network aggregates - Job-posting feeds - Social-media sentiment - LLM-extracted earnings-call signal - Satellite imagery of ports ::: {.verdict} Daily-frequency. Open to data-poisoning attacks. ::: ::: ::: ::: ```{=html}

Where this matters

A non-exhaustive map of central-bank nowcast and big-data programs documented in BIS annual reports 2020–2024.
Federal Reserve
FRBNY Nowcast
Real-time GDP signal from a dynamic factor model with high-frequency inputs.
European Central Bank
BEAR · BBE Nowcast
Bayesian VAR plus big-data inflation indicators ingesting scanner-price feeds.
Bank of England
Nowcast Suite
Mixed-frequency model combining card-spend feeds and Companies House data.
Bank of Japan
UTokyo Daily Price Project
Web-scraped point-of-sale prices feeding into a daily inflation indicator.
Riksbank · Sweden
SEB Nowcaster
Cross-references VAR output gap estimates with real-time payment flows.
Bank for Int'l Settlements
BIS Big Data Initiative
Coordinates AI/ML inputs, supply-chain text feeds, and satellite indicators.
``` ::: {.lede .no-dropcap} In 2024, the U.S. Treasury Department warned that "data poisoning, data leakage, and data integrity attacks can take place at any stage of the AI development and supply chain." The same year, a Russian information operation called Pravda showed the world the warning was concrete. The American Sunlight Project documented 3.6 million auto-generated articles published across the network in 2024 alone. The articles were not designed to be read by humans; many of the sites lacked basic functionality. They were designed to be ingested by the large-language models and search summarizers that have begun to source the open web. ::: ::: {.pravda} ### What 3.6 million articles look like ::: {.subtitle} Each dot represents 1,000 Pravda articles published in 2024. Highlighted dots: 92 articles cited by mainstream LLM chatbots in Newsguard's audit. :::
Auto-generated article (1,000 each)Cited in chatbot audit
::: ::: {.lede .no-dropcap} Newsguard ran an independent audit. Across 450 separate prompts to ten of the most popular AI chatbots, those models referenced 92 distinct Pravda articles. One in three returned Kremlin narratives directly. The Russian propagandist John Mark Dougan, on Russian state media, did not bother to obscure the strategy: "By pushing these Russian narratives from the Russian perspective, we can actually change worldwide AI." A central bank's nowcast pipeline is the same kind of system as a chatbot's retrieval layer. Less famous, consequential in a way a chatbot is not. :::
::: {.lede} ## And the threshold is collapsing Until recently, "data poisoning at scale" sounded like a problem requiring nation-state resources. October 2025 changed that. Researchers at Anthropic, the UK AI Safety Institute, and the Alan Turing Institute published an empirical lower bound that surprised the field: the number of poisoned documents needed to plant a working backdoor in a large language model **does not grow with the size of the model.** ::: ::: {.threshold-callout} ::: {.threshold-number} 250 ::: ::: {.threshold-label} documents. ::: ::: {.threshold-detail} That is the threshold required to backdoor a 13-billion-parameter language model. Below 250, attacks fail. Above, they succeed. The threshold is the same whether the model has 600 million parameters or 13 billion. The threshold is the same whether the training corpus is 4× compute-optimal or 100× larger. ::: ::: {.callout-source} Souly et al., October 2025 · "Poisoning Attacks on LLMs Require a Near-Constant Number of Poison Samples" · arXiv 2510.07192 ::: ::: ::: {#chart-souly .cell execution_count=4} ::: {#chart-souly-1 .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {#chart-souly-2 .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {.scale-blocks} ::: {.scale-block} ::: {.scale-block-num} 250 ::: ::: {.scale-block-label} documents needed for a working backdoor on a 13B model. ::: ::: ::: {.scale-block .scale-mid} ::: {.scale-block-num} 14,400 ::: ::: {.scale-block-label} separate models that the Pravda operation produced enough material to poison in 2024 alone. ::: ::: ::: {.scale-block .scale-warn} ::: {.scale-block-num} ~$200 ::: ::: {.scale-block-label} estimated cost to generate 250 plausibly economic news documents using current open-weight LLMs. ::: ::: ::: ::: {.lede .no-dropcap} The implication for monetary policy is direct. A central bank ingesting scraped public-web data does not need to defend against a billion-document operation. It needs to defend against 250 deliberately placed documents in the right corner of the open web. The cost of producing them is now trivially small relative to the position size such an attack could justify. :::
::: {.lede .no-dropcap style="text-align: center; margin-bottom: 0;"} ## We modeled it. ::: ::: {.scrolly} ::: {.scrolly-narrative} ::: {.scrolly-step data-state="realistic"} ### Start with the model the Fed actually uses. The standard New Keynesian model has three equations: a Phillips curve, an Euler-equation IS curve, and a Taylor rule. The textbook version assumes households can adjust spending instantly, prices are fully forward-looking, and the central bank moves in one shot. The empirical literature has spent twenty years documenting that none of this is true. Smets and Wouters' Bayesian-estimated DSGE model, which has become the workhorse for academic macro and the Fed's own structural analysis, layers in three frictions: consumption habit, price indexation, and interest rate smoothing. A standardized data-poisoning shock pushes the Fed's perceived output gap up by one percentage point. The Taylor rule alone would call for a hike of roughly fifty basis points. Watch what actually happens. ::: ::: {.scrolly-step data-state="cumulative"} ### The cost is what economists call welfare loss, and it more than triples. The impact response barely moves. But the path keeps drifting. Watch the policy-rate panel from quarter zero out to quarter eight. The Fed undershoots, persistently, the entire window. Aggregate the deviations across the policy rate, inflation, and the output gap through the standard New Keynesian welfare loss function and you get a single number. Under sustained attack with a naive Fed, the loss is more than three times what it would be without the attack. The frictions did not defend the economy. They displaced the cost in time. A contemporary Fed, ingesting one bad signal, does not over-react now. It pays for two years. ::: ::: {.scrolly-step data-state="defended"} ### Now turn down the Fed's trust in the signal. The model has one knob the Fed controls: the weight it places on the raw nowcast in its perception filter. At weight one, the Fed takes the signal at face value. At weight zero, it ignores the raw signal entirely and relies only on its own model-based prior. Hold the empirical Phillips slope and Smets-Wouters habit fixed, and turn the filter weight down to ten percent. The attack response collapses by roughly a third on impact and even more cumulatively. The Fed does not need to ignore the signal entirely to defend itself; it needs to stop trusting it. The defense is not free. A Fed that down-weights its nowcast under attack also down-weights it during a real shock. ::: ::: ::: {.scrolly-chart} ::: {.scrolly-chart-inner}
::: ::: ::: ::: {.bigstat} ::: {.number .counter data-target="3.2" data-suffix="×" data-start="1.0"} 3.2× ::: ::: {.label} Welfare loss under sustained attack, relative to the no-attack baseline, when the Fed treats its nowcast at face value. A defended Fed brings the ratio back to 1.0×. ::: ::: {.callout-source} Author calculations · Smets-Wouters posterior · NK welfare loss L = var(π) + 0.5·var(ygap) ::: ::: ::: {#cell-chart-welfare-compare .cell execution_count=5} ::: {#chart-welfare-compare .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` Welfare loss with and without attack, across three Fed filter regimes. The defended regime (K = 0) eliminates the attack-induced loss entirely. The cost is that the Fed becomes less responsive to genuine real shocks, raising baseline loss modestly. ::: :::
::: {.lede} ## Move the sliders yourself Below is the full economy in your hands. Drag the sliders to set how the Fed operates and how the economy behaves, then watch what happens when an attacker slips a one-percentage-point fake reading into the data feed. You don't need to know what a Phillips curve is. The readout under the chart translates everything into rate moves and inflation in plain English. ::: ```{=html}
0.15 · realistic
Lower = stickier prices, the Fed has more time to react. Higher = inflation moves quickly. US data points to about 0.15.
0.7 · realistic
0 = households turn on a dime. 0.7 = realistic, US households change habits gradually. 0.9 = very sticky spending.
1.00 · naive
1.0 = full trust. The Fed acts on the feed at face value. 0.0 = full defense, the Fed ignores the feed and uses its own internal model. The middle is partial filtering.
```
::: {.lede} ## The defense, and what it costs Svensson and Woodford showed two decades ago that when economic measurements are especially noisy or uncertain, the optimal policy is to pay them less attention. In the language of the Kalman filter, the central bank should put a smaller weight on the raw signal and a larger weight on its own model-based prior. The same idea applies, exactly, to the data-poisoning case. Filter harder, attack hurts less. But filtering harder also means the Fed is less responsive to genuine shocks. A central bank that ignores its nowcast under attack also ignores it during a real productivity shift, a real demand shock, a real disinflation. The defense has a cost, and the size of the cost depends on what you think the probability of attack actually is. ::: ::: {.lede .no-dropcap} We compute, at every parameter configuration in the grid, a crossover probability: the minimum perceived attack probability at which paying the filtering cost beats remaining naive. At the empirical Phillips slope and Smets-Wouters habit, the crossover sits around 25 percent. If you think the chance of a sustained, undetected nowcast-poisoning attack against the Fed in any given year is meaningfully above one in four, you should be filtering. If you think it is well below, you should not be. That is a question for cyber threat intelligence, not for the macroeconomist. The model can tell you the breakeven probability. It cannot tell you which side of breakeven we are on. :::
::: {.lede} ## Three policy pillars A defended Fed is the model's prescription. It is also the easiest reform to implement, because it requires nothing of anyone outside the FOMC. The harder reforms work upstream of the Fed, on the integrity of the data itself. The original memo proposed three. **Cryptographic feed signatures.** Every JSON or CSV nowcast feed the Fed ingests should originate from a hardware security module. The HSM holds the signing key in tamper-resistant hardware; NIST treats it as the gold standard for data integrity. The European Central Bank already requires this for its statistical data exchange. The cost is real: a 2023 market survey put the average HSM at thirteen thousand dollars per unit. The benefit is a tamper-evident audit trail that makes silent poisoning attacks much harder to execute. **Uncertainty-adaptive Taylor coefficients.** Make the model's prescription a rule. When the dispersion across nowcast inputs widens, the Fed should automatically down-weight noisy indicators in its policy response. This is exactly the Svensson-Woodford framework operationalized. The risk is recursion: if the dispersion measures themselves can be manipulated, the defense becomes the attack surface. **Public provenance ledgers.** Publish the full ingestion log: every input, its source, its timestamp, its weight. The Russian Pravda operation was uncovered by the American Sunlight Project, an outside group with no special access. A public ledger lets external auditors do the same job for the Fed. Shayne Longpre and co-authors have argued for a multi-stakeholder data provenance standard "akin to the W3 consortium." The risk is the inverse of the previous one: full transparency tells adversaries which inputs carry the most policy weight, and lets them target accordingly. No single pillar is sufficient. Together they form the layered defense that the model says is worth paying for. :::
::: {.method-note} ### About this study The model is a New Keynesian DSGE solved in Julia (MacroModelling.jl), validated to machine precision against the original Dynare 6.3 implementation. The main calibration uses Smets-Wouters posterior parameters: Phillips slope κ = 0.15, consumption habit h = 0.7, price indexation χ_p = 0.5, interest rate smoothing ρ_i = 0.7. The Fed's perception filter is Kalman-style: `gap_perceived = (1 − K) · ρ_p · gap_perceived[-1] + K · (ygap + ν + attack)`. The 80-quarter welfare loss is the sum of squared IRF contributions across three shocks: productivity, monetary policy, and attack. The full methodology brief, the lit review with citations, and a non-economist primer are linked in [the project repository](https://github.com/jblakeslee89/poison-dsge). All code is open source under MIT license. This page is the public-facing data story. The peer-review version is in preparation. ::: ::: {.story-footer} :::: {style="text-align:center"} **Adversarial Nowcasting and Monetary Policy** :::: A working paper by John Blakeslee · April 2026 · [Code on GitHub](https://github.com/jblakeslee89/poison-dsge) · [Companion primer (PDF)](../docs/companion_primer.pdf) · [Methodology brief (PDF)](../docs/methodology_brief.pdf) :::
